Posted February 8, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: I would never waste anyone’s time with a denunciation of marijuana prohibition in the world’s nastier police states. Indeed, marijuana prohibition is entirely consistent with the policies of North Korea or Iraq.

On the other hand, marijuana prohibition in countries that have a political tradition based on individual freedom, especially Anglo-Saxon cultures, is not merely wrong, but a betrayal of the principles on which the countries are supposedly governed.

Marijuana prohibition is also particularly hypocritical in the broader moral and social context of these countries. After all, their cultures are generally liberal regarding personal freedom, and the people use and abuse alcohol, tobacco and a wide variety of pharmaceuticals in vast quantities.

Ultimately, the fact that the marijuana reform movement is based on the fundamental principles of these countries --liberty and limited government interference in the lives of individual – assures the victory of freedom. Moreover the glaring hypocrisy of marijuana prohibition in these cultures undermines the moral authority of the laws and any government that supports them.

The stories below illustrate both of these points – ad nauseum. Most of the UK papers carried this, so it is definitely big news.

What this really means is that those whose race and class largely exempt them from the laws now have another loophole and the police have more arbitrary power.

In many jurisdictions, when dealing with people of the better sort, the police just seize the contraband, usually throwing it away, thus saving everyone time and money, except for the cost of the lost cannabis, of course.

Other times they may give these people " cautions " – which is what is being covered here. Cautions are given after a person has been arrested and taken to a police station -- if they plead guilty.

Others are still criminally charged and sometimes sentenced to jail. This will not change.

In a twist worthy of Animal Farm, a Labor government is adding even more class and race distinctions to the enforcement of marijuana prohibition in the UK. How perfect that the son the Justice Minister benefits from their new enlightenment.)

Straw relaxes law on cannabis possession
By Ian Burrell, Home Affairs Correspondent
February 8, 2001
The Government moved yesterday to relax the laws on the use of cannabis by pledging to remove the " stigma " attached to hundreds of thousands of people caught in possession of the drug.
See
UK " Gangbusters Are Warning The Government That Going Soft On Cannabis Laws Will Trigger A New Drugs Crisis. "
and
The DEA Is Telling UK Narks That " Britain's drug barons are exporting home grown, high grade cannabis to Holland in exchange for Dutch ecstasy. "

In an important move towards liberalisation of the law, the Home Office said people cautioned for having cannabis would no longer have to declare their offence to employers or immigration officials as their offences would be immediately treated as " spent ".

In another concession to liberalisation, the Home Office said it was prepared to consider new sentencing guidelines to ensure that people found guilty of supplying drugs to friends were not treated by the courts as " professional dealers ".

The proposal, which will affect hundreds of thousands of people, formed part of a largely hostile government response to an independent report by the Police Foundation calling for reform of Britain's drugs laws.
See
The Economist Magazine Says Prince Charles' Police Foundation Will Recommend UK " Depenalize " Small Amount Of Cannabis

Although the Government rejected recommendations to lower the drug classification of cannabis, ecstasy and LSD, its willingness to change the law on cautioning was welcomed by drugs advice groups.

Mike Goodman, director ofRelease, said: " This has been a big problem. We have had cases where people have said they have not got a criminal record but employers have done a police search and the caution has come up.
(MarijuanaNews note: Releaseis an outstanding organization. Their web site says, " RELEASE provides a range of services dedicated to meeting the health, welfare and legal needs of drugs users and those who live and work with them. The organization was founded in 1967 in response to the growing number of young people who were coming into contact with illegal drugs. With the voluntary support of many young professionals, Release established the first ever national drugs helpline and has maintained its pivotal role in the drugs and legal advice field and now operates a number of service programmes ".

They also advocate reform.

Mike Goodman is a good man.)

In its response to the Police Foundation report, the Home Office said: " The Government have accepted that there is a ... problem relating to the stigma attached to possessing a caution; for example when asked to confirm the existence of a criminal record by a prospective employer. We have consulted on proposals to apply the provisions of the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 to cautions on the basis that they should become spent immediately. "

The Home Office said it was seeking a " suitable legislative vehicle " to introduce the change.

More than 89,000 people were convicted of possessing cannabis in 1998, the most recent year for which figures are available. Of these, 54 per cent were given a caution at the discretion of the arresting police officer.

In 1999, 266,000 people received cautions for a variety of criminal offences. Under the current system, cautions remain on the police national computer for five years and can be used by the courts in sentencing for further offences for three years.

The proposed changes would still allow the courts to consider previous cautions when sentencing but would remove the obligation on individuals to declare the offences to employers and officials.
See
More Calls for Legalizing Cannabis Come from Influential Sources In Scotland and London. -- 2 Articles

People seeking a career in the law or in the police or prison services will still be required to declare cautions, although they will not automatically be barred from employment.

Viscountess Runciman of Doxford, lead author of the Police Foundation report, said she was pleased the Government had recognised the importance of removing the stigma from cannabis cautions, but was " disappointed " that ministers had rejected most of its 81 recommendations, including the removal of custodial sentences for cannabis, ecstasy and LSD possession.
See
New UK Survey Shows Teen Drugs Use Down And Marijuana Legalization Would Not Increase Use. -- 2 Articles
and
Blair To Declare War On Cannabis – What Prohibition Is Really All About. War On Half The Youth Of The UK

Straw tries to soften rejection of drug report
Users given cautions need not tell employers
Excerpted from The Guardian
By Alan Travis, home affairs editor
February 8, 2001

The government yesterday tried to take the sting out of its rejection of a report urging reform of drugs laws by announcing that the 50,000 offenders cautioned each year for cannabis possession will not be given criminal records in the future.

Ministers announced that they intend to change the legislation on the rehabilitation of offenders to ensure that the cautions 266,000 people receive each year for all offences, including drugs, will not have to be declared to employers or when travelling abroad.
(MarijuanaNews note: Especially to DEAland.)

They also agreed they would review sentencing to ensure that those who are caught selling drugs to a few friends are not treated as harshly as professional dealers.

The Home Office response yesterday said it was necessary to keep a prison sentence on the statute book for simple possession of cannabis as " an important backstop to ensure that defendants appear in court " and " as an incentive to treatment " ….
See
The 50th Anniversary of The Publishing Of Orwell’s 1984
Analysis By Richard Cowan

One result of the report, however, is that an anti-drug driving publicity campaign - similar to the familiar drink- drive advertisements - is to be launched by the transport authorities.
See
UK Study on Marijuana and Driving Again Shows That It Is Not A Significant Factor in Accidents. Should We Arrest People for Being Tired?

But the rejection of the landmark report dismayed drugs law reform campaigners.

The head of the inquiry, Lady Runciman, said: " It is disappointing that a real opportunity for constructive dialogue and incremental change has been missed. All our most far-reaching recommendations have been rejected. At no point has the rationale underlying the proposals been addressed. It leaves us with a law that is out of touch with reality. I believe this is good report. Its time will come. "
(MarijuanaNews note: With all due respect to Lady Runciman, The Police Foundation report was much too timid. See
Chief Police Officers From One Of UK's Busiest Forces Say Drugs Laws Don't Work And Legalisation Is 'The Obvious Alternative Approach.'
and
UK Drugs Expert Criticizes Proposed 2 Gram Limit On " Depenalization " of Cannabis As " completely unrealistic as a limit. " -- Letter To London Times

Perhaps they thought that advocating a realistic policy along Dutch lines would politically unrealistic. In fact, their half-measures have been rejected.)

David Winnick, a Labour backbench member of the Commons home affairs committee, agreed with Lady Runciman, adding that he hoped a more sensible debate on drugs would emerge after the pressures of the forthcoming general election campaign had passed.
(MarijuanaNews note: A national Parliamentary election is expected in the Spring, probably May.)

Excerpted from The London Times
February 8, 2001
By Richard Ford, Home Correspondent

Drug cautions go off the record

The plans announced by Jack Straw yesterday will be particularly important to thousands of young people including his own son who have been cautioned for minor drugs offences.

Until now, a police caution, reprimand or final warning has been deemed to be part of a criminal record. That meant it had to be declared if raised at a job interview and could lead to a rejection of visa applications. Such warnings are never expunged under the

Rehabilitation of Offenders Act, 1974, but the Home Office now says that they should be considered as spent immediately. The police will still keep a record of cautions and may use them as evidence in future criminal proceedings.

In its response to the drugs inquiry, the Home Office said: _The Government has accepted that there is a problem relating to the stigma attached to possessing a caution; for example when asked to confirm the existence of a criminal record by a prospective employer._

Cautions are given after a person has been arrested. He or she is taken to a police station and, if they admit the offence, are formally cautioned. Reprimands and final warnings are issued to offenders aged between 10 and 17. A total of 266,100 people were cautioned in 1999, about a quarter of them for drugs offences.

The most public cases of caution and reprimand in recent years involved William Straw and Euan Blair, elder son of the Prime Minister. William Straw was cautioned in 1998 after admitting selling cannabis to a journalist for 10 Pounds.

Euan Blair, 16, was reprimanded for being drunk and incapable in Leicester Square last year.

(MarijuanaNews note: And on medical marijuana, the Blair government is steadfastly defending the pharmaceutical industry against the threat of patients using a plant.)


Leeds, United Kingdom

CANNABIS ON PRESCRIPTION MAY BE ALLOWED

If cannabis had therapeutic benefits, the Government would allow it to be prescribed, a Home Office Minister says.
(MarijuanaNews note: This story misses the point entirely. Obviously any government is going to allow the use of a pharmaceutical based on cannabis after it has gone through its regulatory ritual. The real news here is that the UK government is going to continue arresting patients who use whole smoked cannabis.)

Charles Clarke made the comments in the Commons, but made it clear the Government would draw a distinction between the therapeutic use of cannabis and its recreational use.

There are currently two trials on the therapeutic benefits of cannabis taking place. One is being carried out by a private company and another by the Home Office.
See
UK To Spend 3 Years And A Million And Half Dollars On Tests
To Find Out If Marijuana Helps MS Patients,
But Will Do No Research To See If Arresting Them Is Harmful.

But he emphasised the Government would only act on the basis of scientific evidence and not on the testimonies of individuals who said cannabis had helped their condition.
(MarijuanaNews note: If such cases were rare, and if most of the patients were not using cannabis for symptomatic relief, of which they are the best judges, then that might make a little sense. However, the UK MS Society estimates that there are already over 1,000 MS patients alone using cannabis illegally.

Ignoring such large numbers is both bad science and bad medicine. Ignoring the fact that these people are being arrested is bad science and bad medicine, and just plain bad, as in evil.)

He said: " We must act on the basis of scientific tests. To get to the position of changing the law we need to have a proper scientific judgment. " Also giving evidence Dr Brian Davis of the Medicines Control Agency Licensing Division said even if the present trials had positive results, more extensive trials would be needed before cannabis could be licensed for therapeutic use.
(MarijuanaNews note: In other words, they are prepared to stall, however long it takes.)

He referred to a study which had shown that cannabis had impaired the fertility of male monkeys.
(MarijuanaNews note: The mind boggles. Even if there was any evidence that the levels of cannabis used by humans was producing a shortage of babies – and there is not – it would still be wildly irrelevant in this context. People are suffering and he is worried about monkey fertility!)
